title: Intelkin
summary: A tool that uses neuroscience to predict how the brain responds to a design before anyone sees it, catching churn risk before launch instead of after.
narrative: Every retention tool on the market today is reactive — it watches what customers do after a feature ships, then reacts once the churn has already happened. I built Intelkin to move that read earlier: it runs a design through Tribe V2, Meta's brain-response model, before any real customer sees it, and returns which cognitive regions are overloaded and where. I dogfooded it on our own Recollab investor demo and it caught three friction points our team had gone blind to after six weeks staring at the same screens — that's the actual argument for the tool, not just the pitch. I'm upfront about the trade-off: it's predicting a general research population's brain responses, not Recollab's specific users, so it's a fast pre-launch signal, not a replacement for testing with real people. It's still a two-piece prototype (a clickable UI shell plus a working terminal pipeline) — the model itself turned out to be the easy part; reading its brain-region output by hand is the real bottleneck, which is why automating that with Claude Vision is the next step, not the model.

title: Langchain Aggregator
summary: Rebuilt a single automated guess at vendor matching into a five-agent system with a person approving every step — 8x faster quote turnaround, zero unapproved outreach across a 5-building trial.
previewPrompt: Tell me about the Recollab Langchain aggregator project.
narrative: Recollab builds software for property managers running large condo buildings, and one gap was blocking a signed contract: when something broke — a leak, an HVAC failure — property managers had no fast way to get multiple vendor quotes in front of them, just phone calls to whoever they already knew. I shipped a first working version in n8n in a week to close the deal, but "nearby" was doing too much work — no distance cap, no license or trade check — and it ran for two days queuing outreach to vendors outside a building's service area before we caught it. Once real customers depended on it, I rebuilt it as a proper multi-agent system: an orchestrator, a vendor-matching agent that checks known trusted vendors first, a vendor-sourcing agent for when there isn't a match, an outreach agent, a quote-aggregation agent, and a follow-up agent — with a person approving every quote and every hire, no exceptions. It ran live across 5 buildings with zero unapproved outreach or hires. The lesson I carry forward: don't ship a matching rule without a specific, testable boundary.
